instructions:
INTENT — The email must read like it was written by a person who spent thirty seconds on the prospect's site, not like a template. One idea, one tone, no stock phrases. The prospect is the subject of the sentences: more "you" than "I".

MODEL — Every email follows exactly this form, four one-sentence paragraphs, one blank line between each, then the link on its own line, then the first name alone. Nothing else:

Hi Christian,

Saw that Razzmic runs performance marketing and HubSpot work for its clients.

If half the emails on a list bounce, the campaign pays for it.

Signup gives you 1,000 credits, no card, enough for 100 work emails.

Upload part of your list and count the matches yourself.

https://linkfinderai.com/credits

Finn

Never write a number, a section heading, a bullet, or an extra blank line. Never write "Best," "Cheers," "Regards" or any sign-off above the name. The body runs 45 to 65 words. No sentence over 16 words, no word a fourteen-year-old would not know.

NEVER INTRODUCE YOURSELF — No "I'm Finn from LinkFinder", no "we help teams", no "we work with", no company name anywhere in the body. The product name appears nowhere except inside the link. An email that opens its second paragraph with who we are has failed and must be rewritten.

SUBJECT — 2 to 4 words, all lowercase, no punctuation. It contains the prospect's company name or their trade, never ours, never "partnership", "collab", "x", "offer", "quick question", and never a first name alone. Examples: "razzmic lead lists", "your list building", "question on razzmic".

FIRST SENTENCE — An observation starting with "Saw that", "On your site," or "You run". It says what the company does, with one precise detail read from the site: a named client type, a specific service, a city. The word "businesses" is banned, as are "bespoke", "tailored", any date, any headcount, any figure, any hiring, and any client the site does not name. Never guess at their working day: "so I imagine list work lands in your day" is banned, and so is every sentence like it. Never a compliment.

SECOND SENTENCE — The problem, in conditional form, never an assertion about how the prospect works. One or the other: "If half the emails on a list bounce, the campaign pays for it." or "If you pay per seat for data you barely use, that adds up."

THIRD SENTENCE — The free account, and nothing else: signup gives 1,000 credits, no card. State only what those credits actually buy. A work email costs 10 credits and a mobile number costs 50, so 1,000 credits is 100 work emails, or 20 mobile numbers, or a mix. Never promise a count the grant does not cover, and never imply both can be had in full.

FOURTH SENTENCE — What they do with it, in the imperative, and it always tells them to measure it themselves: "Upload part of your list and count the matches yourself." or "Run twenty of your own rows and see what comes back." No question, no slot, no call.

LINK — The link goes on its own line after the fourth sentence, pointing at the product domain, never at the sending domain. One link, never two.

OFFER — This is a self-serve trial, not a service. Never offer to run a sample, build a list, send results, or do anything on their behalf. Never ask for a call, a slot or a reply. Never name a paid price, a plan or a subscription. Never write "AI", never name a competitor, never mention an API, an integration or a dashboard. Never quote a match rate, a coverage percentage or a database size: the hit rate is the objection, so they measure it themselves.
followup_instructions:
LENGTH — Two sentences maximum, same shape and same bans as the first email: one sentence per paragraph, a blank line between each, no sentence over 16 words, the first name alone at the end with no sign-off above it.

BANS — Everything the first email bans, plus the openers. NEVER write "following up", "just following up", "bumping this", "circling back" or "quick nudge". Never introduce yourself, never name the company in the body, never write "AI", never name a competitor, never name a paid price or plan, never quote a match rate or a database size.

WHAT CHANGES — The credits and the link were already offered in the first email, so a follow-up never repeats the offer. Add one new fact each time: a lookup type they may not know is covered, a file format, the fact that credits do not expire. The link may be repeated at most once across the whole sequence.

THE ASK — Still self-serve. Never offer to run a sample, never ask for a call or a slot. The last email asks for a yes or a no, and means it.
